utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I first wish to apologise on behalf of my colleagues and myself for this delay, but it was due to other official engagements affecting the Tribunal, which is an international body, and obviously has certain obligations which require the presence of the judges. I wish to welcome the accused -- do you hear me, General Blaskic. GENERAL BLASKIC: Good afternoon, your Honours, I can hear you very well indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If General Blaskic can hear me there is every chance parties can hear me as well. We can proceed to the continuation of our hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours and counsel. We would request, Mr. President, to proceed in a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. As I do not know exactly why you are asking for a closed session, I assume it is in order to explain to us why you are asking for a closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I say that for the benefit of the public and the observers. I do not wish them to have the impression that immediately the Prosecutor asks for a closed session that we adopt a closed session, but I now understand the reasons. I turn to my colleagues, I have their approval. Under those conditions, we can pass on to a closed session now. A private session or a closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: A private session is sufficient for the purposes of my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, private session, Mr. Registrar. (In private session) [Confidentiality lifted by order of Chamber] Very well, Mr. Prosecutor, we are in private session now. I assume that you have something to explain to us which requires a private session. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Some time ago, as a result of events which the court is already familiar with, I was informed by the next Prosecution witness that he wished to proceed in testifying in a closed session. The Prosecutor's Office fully supports his request for the reasons which I will explain and for the reasons which, if the court is desirous, he will explain. In our communications with the Defence to notify them of which witness we were going to call today, I identified the witness to the Defence and I also informed the Defence that we would be requesting a closed session. On Thursday, the 12th, I received a communication back from Mr. Hayman informing me that they would oppose that request absent knowing fully the bases for making that request and I subsequently filed a copy of Mr. Hayman's letter to me as attachment A by consent with counsel. The following day, I met with Mr. Hayman and we discussed some of the bases for the request for a closed session, and I was informed that counsel would discuss the matter amongst themselves upon the return of Mr. Nobilo from Zagreb and I would be informed of their decision. I was informed moments ago that the Defence is not able to agree to a closed session for the witness, and, therefore, I am pursuing my application which I filed on Friday for protective measures for this witness, specifically for a request to proceed with the witness's testimony in a closed session pursuant to Rule 75(B)(ii) and pursuant to 79(A)(ii) and A(iii). So now, Mr. President, if the court pleases, I am prepared to expand on the bases for this request, if the court wishes me to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Following the receipt of the statement that was taken by the Office of the Prosecutor and submitted to the Defence in early May, the complete statement of the witness was distributed through President Tudjman's office and by President Tudjman at the presidential palace on or about 6 May 1997. What followed, after the distribution of the statement of Mr. Mesic was the public pillorying of Mr. Mesic in the media. The media campaign was orchestrated at the highest levels of the State of Croatia. Mr. Mesic was branded an traitor and the media incited the public against the witness. Following that incitement, and I have submitted some examples of that with the court and previous filings, Mr. Mesic received a constant stream of threatening phone calls. Both he and his family received phone calls which threatened his life, threatened the lives of his family members. Following the unfortunate publication in the press of his statement, Mr. Mesic was required -- obligated -- to defend himself in the media and he made numerous appearances in the media trying to blunt the orchestrated attack that was being mounted against him. It was certainly quite a natural reaction from someone who had been attacked in the press, but it was one that was forced upon him unfortunately, by President Tudjman and the serious violation of Tribunal confidentiality. The fact that he responded to these virulent attacks is not in any way a waiver or intended to be a waiver for his request to testify before this Tribunal and to testify in a session that afforded him protection; that is, a closed session. As part of the State campaign that has been mounted against him, the witness believes now that he is under constant surveillance and he is being followed. Subsequently he received threats from individuals who were responsible -- personal and direct threats -- from individuals who were responsible for the killing of civilians in Pakras Polanje and the killings of a prominent family in Zagreb. These threats were made by persons who were admitted murderers and whose convictions were overturned by the Croatian Supreme Court for a violation relating to non-representation by counsel at the time they made their statements to the authorities. Subsequently, Mr. President, an oblique threat was made against the witness in a most recent past, within the last three weeks, by President Tudjman. Mr. Mesic believes the testimony he is prepared to present to your Honours is valuable testimony, and that the efforts that I have summarised have been orchestrated by persons in the highest positions of power in Croatia in order to prevent him from testifying before you. He believes, Mr. President, and the Prosecutor supports him in this belief, that he and his family are at considerable personal risk if his testimony is made public -- and if his request to proceed in a closed session is denied. Mr. President, and your Honours, Mr. Mesic is prepared to testify about the matters that I have summarised briefly, if the court so desires. That concludes my comments, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Hayman, Mr. Nobilo, you are opposed to a closed session. Who is Mr. Mesic actually, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Mesic is a well known political figure in the former Yugoslavia. He was the last President of the presidency in the former Yugoslavia before Yugoslavia essentially disintegrated or fell apart. Mr. Mesic was a founder -- not a founder but he was instrumental in HDZ political affairs. He was a person who was instrumental in the founding of the HDZ political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He has occupied the position of Prime Minister in the Republic of Croatia. He has a variety of high-level Government official positions in Croatia. He is and was an intimate of Franjo Tudjman and he is currently the head -- separated from the HDZ and has formed a separate political party in Opposition to the HDZ in Croatia. I can give greater detail but I think I have hit a significant number of highlights of his distinguished career.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you are opposed on behalf of General Blaskic to testimony in closed session. What are your reasons, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you tried to reach an agreement -- have you had discussions over this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, we had a very short conversation so that we did not touch upon the substance of the issue. But I will be brief. As you know, the Defence has never, so far, opposed any kind of protection measures, because we are aware that people and particularly those in Bosnia-Herzegovina may, at times, be exposed to certain security risks and out of the respect for the integrity of each witness, we never opposed such measures. But the reason why we are disputing it this time is our fear that politicians may draw the Tribunal into some kind of political manipulations so that the Tribunal may become an instrument in the political disputes between political parties in Croatia. Therefore, we are concerned in protecting the integrity of this Tribunal, namely, everything that Mr. Mesic said in his statement for the Prosecutor has -- he has repeated in numerous interviews. I have collected maybe 200 of those interviews. Not a single point that he made in the statement for the Office of the Prosecutor exists which has not been repeated on innumerable occasions. After the publication of his statement, which the Prosecutor places in a rather embarrassing context, because the Prosecutor said that he provided that statement to the Defence after which it was published, but it is also worth noting that it was not a confidential statement -- after the publication of that statement, Mr. Mesic has made at least twice or three times as many interviews, which he used in his political struggle. Furthermore, before going to The Hague, Mr. Mesic promised to give an interview to the journalist about his testimony in The Hague and he said that, after his return from The Hague, at the end of this week, he would grant an interview to a well known Croatian weekly. Therefore, in my view, this is a kind of a political ploy. I think that Croatia, as a legal State, is stable enough to protect all its citizens' security and safety, and he is a public figure, a politician, he is accustomed to debates and discussions and I assure you he is very skilful in that respect and he cannot be intimidated through political debate. As for specific threats made by persons who committed murders in Pakras Polanje against whom proceedings have been dropped, even that is not correct, because those persons are in Croatian detention and criminal proceedings are under way against those persons, so I cannot see how they could have threatened Mr. Mesic. Also the allegation that Tudjman threatened Mr. Mesic has not been explained in any way, so that we cannot comment on it. To sum up, I feel that the security of Mr. Mesic is not in jeopardy, that all the allegations referred to by the Prosecutor regarding statements made by Mr. Mesic are such that he has made them repeatedly to the press and this only makes the work of the Defence more difficult, because the question is how could we use the information Mr. Mesic will give to verify that information, which we have to do -- to verify the statements through people he has worked with in the Croatian leadership. If the hearing is closed, the question is how we can use that information and that data. Furthermore, there is no record of Mr. Mesic requesting any police protection because of any threats made to him. He is a very well known figure and I cannot imagine that his personal safety could have been threatened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you have something to add before the judges make their ruling?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. In the motion that I filed on Friday, on page 4, footnote number 2, I informed the Chamber that Mr. Mesic intends to testify publicly in the Dokmanovic case -- this week -- and obviously the interests in the Dokmanovic case are different than the interests in the testimony that the court may receive and will receive in this particular case. I have conferred with Mr. Mesic, I have asked Mr. Mesic if in fact he has made statements about his willingness to talk to his press after his arrival in The Hague and he said that he has and it relates to his public testimony in the Dokmanovic case. So, I think that we should put those statements of Mr. Mesic's willingness to talk to the press in context with his anticipated public testimony that will occur later this week in a different case. Those are my comments, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: May I add two comments, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is not customary, Mr. Hayman, but, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The first would be it would be helpful if we could be served with the application that was filed on Friday. We have never received it. It would help us speak more directly perhaps to the Prosecutor's assertions, including the assertion made in footnote 4 which we were not aware of in even the most general sense, until Mr. Nobilo started to get phone calls from members of the news media in Zagreb asking him about Mr. Mesic's upcoming testimony, which he declined to comment on in any way, shape or fashion. The fact that Mr. Mesic has an appointment with the news media to talk about his testimony in this other case raises a rather obvious question, and that is, he is going to be asked, "Did you testify in the Blaskic case?" Apparently, he is going to lie to the Croatian news media and say, "No, I did not; I was here to testify in a different case", and I query if the Tribunal should be a party to that type of fraud and deception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I turn first towards my colleagues -- no questions? We are going to withdraw and discuss the point. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: After having deliberated, the judges have decided unanimously that Mr. Mesic's testimony will be in closed session. Mr. Registrar, we can move from a private session into a closed session (In closed session) [Confidentiality lifted by order of Chamber]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I raise a second point that was part of our discussions last Friday with Mr. Hayman? If I can identify what the problem is and the solution at the same time, I would like to do that at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, it is very pleasing for this Tribunal to the hear one of the parties raising -- not only raising a problem but also providing a solution to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it came to my attention when I was talking to the witness that Mr. Mesic has in the past been represented by Mr. Nobilo. He has been his counsel in other issues in other litigation. That raised in my mind a potential conflict of interest with the cross-examination by Mr. Nobilo of Mr. Mesic, and, in order to avoid any possible point should there be a conviction and on appeal of a conflict of interest existing between Mr. Nobilo cross-examining his former client, I identify that problem to Mr. Hayman. Mr. Hayman and I had a conversation briefly before we came to court and I was informed that Mr. Blaskic is prepared to waive any potential conflict of interest, should Mr. Nobilo conduct the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President, we can put that waiver on the record, if necessary. I would note, though, that months ago the Defence advised the Prosecution and the court that Mr. Nobilo -- that Mr. Mesic had been a client of Mr. Nobilo's, so that is in the record. That is not something that has been concealed. In fact it was affirmatively disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First, thank you for this clarification. First, we note, and the Registrar will ensure that everything is put into the transcript, stating that the General has given up his right to invoke this issue later on. There may be reasons for appeal, although that is not the main reason. I would also like to express my concern whether it might be more efficient if Mr. Hayman were to conduct the cross-examination. Would that not be even better -- a better guarantee, subject to you being given some time if it was Mr. Nobilo who prepared it? What do you think, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We think the waiver is efficient and in light of the waiver either one of us can conduct the cross-examination. In reality there are many documents in the Croatian language which Mr. Nobilo will potentially be using so he has prepared the cross so I expect him to conduct the cross-examination, with leave of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleagues at the bench. (Pause). Also unanimously, the judges have decided that they would accept the suggestions both by the Prosecution and the Defence and the accused. Therefore, Mr. Nobilo will conduct the cross-examination, since the accused has given -- has waived his right to any challenge later on, on that score. Do you have a third problem, Mr. Harmon, for which of course you would also have a solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My only request in clarification, Mr. President, is that General Blaskic actually state affirmatively for the record that he is prepared to waive the conflict of interest. Counsel has indicated he is prepared to do so but we have not heard from General Blaskic yet on that particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am very pleased to hear General Blaskic -- sometimes I speak to him directly, but perhaps I could ask him more specifically in this case to rise and to say that you give up any right for appeal, because of this possible conflict of interest that might exist between Mr. Nobilo's position, who was the former counsel of Mr. Mesic and the current position of Mr. Nobilo which allows him to conduct the cross-examination. Please state your case clearly and out loud. GENERAL BLASKIC: Your Honours, I feel rather embarrassed to speak after your ruling on this issue. I know that Mr. Stjepan Mesic was a client of my attorney Mr. Nobilo and I waive any potential legal objections regarding possible conflict of interest in that connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General Blaskic. Mr. Harmon, are you completely satisfied and do you have a fourth question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I have no fourth question and I am completely satisfied, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you might now ask the Registrar to have the witness brought in, who will be called by his name, because this is a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you want me to summarise before the witness steps into the courtroom what his testimony will cover?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, before he comes into the courtroom, you should given us the general outline of the testimony. Of course, subject to your using that for something else later on. We want to be careful that your summary brings out the things you are going to emphasise later on. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As I touched upon briefly, the next witness, Mr. Mesic, is an important political figure in the history of the fall of Yugoslavia, the disintegration of Yugoslavia and he has played an important role in both Croatian politics and the politics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Rather than recount the various highlights of his distinguished career now, I am going to ask him to summarise those, so you will be familiar with who he is when he comes before you. He is going to testify about the development of the HDZ political party, both the founding of it in Croatia and the founding of it in Bosnia, and he will discuss the relationship between the HDZ party in Bosnia and the party in Croatia. Because he was a confidante of Franjo Tudjman, the current President of the Republic of Croatia, he has had an opportunity to hear Mr. Tudjman's views about Bosnia and about Bosnian Muslims. He will convey to you what Dr Tudjman's views are in respect of both those topics. He will testify about President Tudjman's dual policy towards Bosnia, one which was a public policy of recognition of the independence of Bosnia, and a clandestine policy to divide Bosnia between Croatia and Serbia. He will testify in that regard about a meeting that took place in 1991 between Slobodan Milosevic and President Tudjman at Kar Zordzivo, after which President Tudjman's clandestine policy to divide Bosnia was implemented. He will also testify about some of the meetings in Zagreb that occurred between Franjo Tudjman and Mate Boban, Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, Ignac Kostroman, and other luminaries of Herceg-Bosna. He will testify about the current laws in Croatia, laws that existed at the time Bosnia was independent, but laws which deal with elections and which tend to undercut the independence of Bosnia. He will testify about Croatian involvement in the Croat Muslim war in Bosnia. He will describe to your Honours the impact of the Vance-Owen peace plan on the thinking of political leaders both in Croatia and in Herceg-Bosna and, lastly, he will testify about conversations he had in respect of Ahmici. That, Mr. President, is a summary of his testimony. His testimony will be relevant to paragraphs 5.0 and 5.1 of the general allegations section of the indictment which allege the existence of an international armed conflict, and his testimony is relevant to all grave breaches counts of the indictment, those counts being 5, 8, 11, 15, 17, and 19. That concludes my introductory remarks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: After the agreement with one of my colleagues, but of course we work in three, so I will speak to my colleague -- I want to consult with him before I ask you a question on a certain point. Did you speak with this witness about Rule 90(F), because this is a closed session; he participated if I understood things correctly at the highest levels of Mr. Tudjman's policies. I do not know if he was involved in any kinds of acts. Did you speak about this with him, because we are going to ask him questions on that subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I did not raise this subpart of Rule 90 with him, because I did not think it applied to him based on the nature of the testimony he was prepared to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. If you are sure, okay, I thank you. We can have Mr. Mesic brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Mr. Mesic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MESIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please remain standing. First, tell us your name and -- your family name and your given names?

utterances.speaker: MR. MESIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Mesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Stjepan Mesic, thank you. The usher will give you a declaration, which is your oath. Please read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MESIC
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. You will answer the Prosecution's questions, who has called you to testify at the International Criminal Tribunal in the trial against General Blaskic, the accused, who is here in this courtroom. You will make your statement freely, in sequences and the Prosecutor will introduce the plan to use and to enter the cohesiveness of what will be said for the judges. STJEPAN MESIC

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Mesic. Mr. Mesic, I am going to ask you a series of questions and I am going to identify the topic and the subject area of those questions. I will then ask you to tell the judges in a narrative form the answers that you have in respect of each of those subject areas. I would like first to begin by asking you to inform the court, if you would, about your background, about your distinguished political career, about the various positions that you have held both in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in the Republic of Yugoslavia when it was one of the Republics of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the positions you have held in the Republic of Yugoslavia since its independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I was born 1934 in Orahovica in Croatia. I completed my elementary school in Orahovica, but this was during the war years, so I spent part of my schooling in Hungary because we had to retreat there as refugees because this was the very end of the war. I graduated from the middle school -- the secondary school in Pozega and then law school in Zagreb. I practised in Narsica and then in Zagreb. I was then a judge for a year, and after that I worked as legal counsel for a company in Zagreb, and then, by accident almost, I was elected a member of Parliament in Zagreb. This was in 1965. At that time, there was only the League of Communists and the Socialist Alliance that could field candidates who would then become members of Parliament if they were elected. There was another possibility, that is, that 100 citizens show up in court and petition for a candidate, and in that manner, this candidate would be on equal footing with the candidates fielded by the Communists. I was the first person during the Communist system who did this, and nobody did it after me. I was the first one -- I brought 100 people there. Then I was elected, and I was unique in that way. I was a member of the Croatian Spring and, after 1971, I was unemployed and I also received a sentence of two years and two months. I spent that sentence in Stara Gradiska. I could not become an attorney, even though I did pass the bar exam, because I was not politically and morally qualified, as it was said in those days. After a while, I was employed finally by an architectural studio to do the legal affairs for them. Its director later retired and then I became a director. The committee of the League of Communists tried to oppose my election. However, it was a small company, so there was not much opposition and I passed. In 1989, I was again elected as a member of Parliament to the same position, which I had held in 1965. I got a mandate to form the Croatian Government and I had to step down as a member of Parliament. After a while, the Parliament -- the Croatian Parliament sent me to Belgrade to become a member of the Presidency and this decision was adopted by the Croatian Parliament. I was first the Vice-President and then President of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There was a lot of difficulties, because the Serb side was opposed to my assuming the position of first Vice-President and then President of the Presidency, even though it was a constitutional provision. After the pressure of the European Troika, I was elected to this position and I was in this position until the end of 1991, whereupon I returned to Zagreb and I was a member of the executive board of the Croatian Democratic Union, and I was in this position until 1992, and in the elections of 1992 I was re-elected to the Croatian Parliament and then I became the President of the Croatian Parliament. Among the political duties which I held during the establishment of the Croatian Democratic Union, I was elected Secretary-General of this party and I was in this position and I was elected to President of the Croatian Government. And now, in a manner of speaking, I am outside of the party institutions. I was a member -- there were three Croatian parties -- Croatian independents -- and a third party fused and I became their President, after having left the ruling party, the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you some clarifications on some of the points you raised. In 1971, you mentioned the Croatian Spring. Can you tell the judges, what was the Croatian Spring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian Spring was actually a movement led by a section of the Communist party, or, rather, the top leadership of the Croatian League of Communists, that is the most progressive part, but it consisted of several parts. One was the students' movement, another was a trade union movement and the third section was a cultural institution known as the Matica Hrvatska, and all three comprised the Croatian Spring.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned that you had been convicted of something. Could you expand on that -- tell the judges exactly what you were convicted of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would sound rather ridiculous nowadays, the charges made against me. Nowadays it is certainly not a criminal offence -- it is not even a misdemeanour, but in those days it was a serious charge, namely, with the formation of the Matica Hrvatska, this cultural association, and its branches in the municipalities, I visited a number of those branch offices -- Slatina, Orahovica, Donje Mikoholjic, Vukovar, and other places, and I said in one of those places that the Croats had paved their way to the Adriatic with their swords in their hands, whereas others had reached that area, either due to our goodness, and we also said that the important thing is for the devil to warm on the fire and not to extinguish it. The third thing I said was that it was certain that the Croats had killed the Yugoslav Ambassador, Rolovic, in Sweden, but that that was not in the interests of the Croatian people, because we were advocating democratisation in Croatia and Yugoslavia and for the adoption of amendments which would lead to a confederal structure and, therefore, the murder, the assassination of the Yugoslavia Ambassador was not in our interests. When I said that, even though the Croats had been the murderers, but I said that the investigation would establish who was behind the act. Of course, when this was interpreted in the judiciary, they found that I had the Serbs in mind, and that I was implying that the Belgrade police was behind this, and this was sufficient to get me a sentence of two years and two months in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Mesic, you said in 1990 you became the Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Can you tell me who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was appointed by the Croatian Parliament, and I was proposed by the President of the Republic, Dr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to turn your attention, Mr. Mesic, to another topic, and that is the development of the HDZ party in Croatia. Could you please tell the judges about the development of that party in Croatia, its evolution, both in terms from a movement to a political party, and its political philosophy as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. With the elimination of the Croatian Spring, that is the end of 1971, all democratic processes in Croatia were halted. They were halted throughout Yugoslavia. Persecution was considerable, and more than 10,000 of us participants in this "Spring" ended up in prison. But an even larger number were left jobless, or were mistreated in other ways. However, that is the way life is, so what happened was that this pressure eased, so that somewhere after 1985 or 1986 we started thinking more about the possibilities of us -- the people of the Opposition -- organising ourselves. I must say that we met in various groups and already in 1988 we started thinking about publishing a journal -- a newspaper -- which would be outside the control of the powers that be. However, with the process of democratisation in Croatia, and in Serbia Milosevic came to power, who manifested aspirations towards expanding the borders of Serbia by abolishing the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina. Amongst us, the process of party formation was accelerated and the first such party was formed in 1989, the Croatian Social Liberal Party, and we, that is, the circle of people, worked on the formation of the Croatian Democratic Community -- using the term "community" so as to avoid the use of the term "a party", because, at that time, it was not allowed, so that the potential danger existed of Parties being abolished and in this way the Croatian Democratic Community would be exempted from that and I think I joined the HDZ a month or two after it was founded. That is, a very large circle of people was involved in the formation of the party, a founding assembly was scheduled, several hundred people attended, but the rumour spread that the police had outlawed the meeting and Franjo Tudjman, together with 56 of his followers, went to a football stadium and proclaimed the formation of the party, the main board was elected and he was elected President of that board , so I did not participate in those very first elections, someone else was elected at the time, Mr. Bobetko, and after that I was elected to that post when I joined the Croatian Democratic Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you describe the political philosophy of the HDZ at its inception and any changes in that philosophy -- any evolution of that philosophy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since all of us Opposition people had opted for democracy and the multi-party system even before the elections, it was clear that the HDZ, in its programme, supported such a multi-party system, and democracy and all democratic processes. At the time when parties were still being formed, they collaborated amongst themselves, even though they were competitors. However, the majority of Parties were shaped or modelled on European political Parties, whereas the HDZ increasingly acquired the characteristics of a movement -- it did not rid itself of this to this day and, even today, it is still a movement. Precisely because the HDZ assumed a monopoly over power, introducing centralisation of power and resources, and precisely because that community did not take the shape of a party, it became an obstacle to the development of democracy, so that we had increasingly the hallmarks of a single party system. The HDZ had a monopoly over power, the other Parties could in no way jeopardise the authority of the HDZ, and most of the decisions, regardless of how productive they may have been or not, they were always adopted, even those which actually halted democratisation in Croatia. Even when the policy towards Bosnia -- Bosnia's turn came, that is the policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, I departed from the policy of the HDZ in those days and that is why in 1994, together with 11 deputies of the Croatian Parliament, I abandoned the HDZ and we formed a new party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, did the philosophy or the character of the HDZ political party change as a result of Slobodan Milosevic's pleas to nationalism -- nationalistic impulses of Serbs who lived in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that there were various factors that influenced the structuring of the HDZ and its policies. One of the most important factors could be said to have been the policies of Slobodan Milosevic, who, with his ultra nationalistic policies in Serbia, contributed to the radicalisation of policies in Slovenia, in Croatia and in Macedonia and, therefore, clearly in Bosnia-Herzegovina; namely, Slobodan Milosevic, by his radical policies, destroyed or abolished the autonomy of Kosovo, the autonomy of Vojvodina; he toppled the leadership of Montenegro; and, clearly, one could not expect a better fate for Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia and Macedonia in the future structuring of the State. This strengthened all those forces which were opposing this radical Serb policy, which looked for like-minded people among the Serbs in Croatia. Unfortunately, we did not manage to win over the Serbs in Croatia to a sufficient degree to oppose these policies of Milosevic's, so that he won considerable influence among the Serbs in Croatia. However, that policy also had an impact on the formation of a rather powerful Croatian radical structure within the HDZ, as well as in other Parties, but certainly less so among the Opposition Parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we might take a short break now, say 15 minutes, and after that we will try to work for about an hour, until about quarter after 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will work until 6 o'clock. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When we took our break, you were telling the judges about the effect that Milosevic's appeals to Serb nationalism had on the HDZ political party in Croatia. Could you please continue describing that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be advised to put on the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is well known that Milosevic came to power in Serbia precisely on this emotional charge. There was resistance in Kosovo that took place due to this Serb policy and he broke this down both in Kosovo and in Vojvodina and continued on in Montenegro and there was a danger after these democratic changes that the same situation would be repeated in Croatia, especially since Milosevic -- not just Milosevic but everybody who followed his policies -- remained constant threats to all the other Republics. Milosevic himself was not interested in any kind of Yugoslavia, either federal or confederal. He was only interested in Serbia and that was a Serbia that would have wider borders. The biggest threat of such a policy was for Croatia, because there was a Serb population in Croatia, which was about 10 per cent of the total population. Part of this population was in all Croatian cities, so there, there was no great danger of any radicalism. However, where there were larger concentrations of Serbs, Milosevic's influence was also greater and a party was created -- an exclusively Serb Democratic party headed by Govan Raskovic, which radicalised Serbs precisely based on the policies of Slobodan Milosevic. At first Serb demands were for cultural autonomy. However, as this nationalist charge rose, the demands also kept rising, so that there was a case of closing roads in Croatia, which was called "the Timber Revolution", and as a member of the Croatian Government, I invited representatives of all Serb communities to sit down together and to look for a solution so that this would stop -- that this process of radicalisation would stop and that we would open up communication lines, roads, and railroads and that the production would go on in the normal way. The representatives of all Serb communities with a Serb majority accepted this except for Milan Babic, who, together with Jovan Raskovic, was in direct contact with Belgrade, that is, with Slobodan Milosevic and he, being in contact with Belgrade, received instructions from Belgrade not to go to such a meeting, and after that, we were turned down by all these Serb municipalities -- majority municipalities. They were told not to negotiate with the Croatian Government and we were brought in a very difficult situation, because the Croatian economy pretty much ground to a halt. There was a problem with health care system, with the social system -- the entire State system, due to this resistance of these radicals, Serb elements, who were receiving instructions exclusively from Belgrade and from Slobodan Milosevic. Since this then became an obstacle for Croatia, the Croatian nationalists also became radicalised and all Serbs became guilty in the eyes of all the Croats and vice versa, so there is a general guilt going on both ways and it is not clear that Slobodan Milosevic was the person who planned all this, so this radicalisation was an obstacle for us to continue with democratic processes. All these processes were halted and this all then led to heating up of the situation and eventually to the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the increasing nationalism impact on the HDZ party and the leader of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. When we established HDZ, I must say that the leadership, in any event, was more democratically oriented. A large number of them were anti-fascists. Starting from Franjo Tudjman, Josip Boljkovac and Manolic -- they were all World War II veterans, so there was no possibility at the time of the establishment of the HDZ to do that. However, later, the policies became more radical and the elements grew stronger, who were looking for their inspiration in the puppet Second World War Croatian State -- puppet of fascist Italy and Germany. It was clear that Croatia today could only be formed on the traditions of anti-fascism. It was created in World War II as a federal unit and this was later confirmed in the constitution, but we still had a number of obstacles coming from those who believed that they could bring back some historical illusions. They did not understand that history was one thing and the present parliament was something completely different and that in history only things that happened really are -- are real. We cannot change that. We can only reinterpret things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Mesic, just for the record and so it is perfectly clear, who was the head of the HDZ political party in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is well known that Franjo Tudjman was elected as the first President of the HDZ. When it was established HDZ had several candidates for President, but Franjo Tudjman won and after that, until now, he has been the President of this party, which is really not a party -- it is a movement. It is a movement which has penetrated all State mechanisms. It controls the media, it is a movement that controls all the economic mechanisms -- everything is centralised. The power is centralised in all its segments. So that this kind of a set-up has really stopped the process of democratisation. However, these processes are going on and things will get better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, I would like to turn your attention to another topic and that is the development of the HDZ political party in Bosnia. First off, do you know approximately when the HDZ political party was established in Bosnia, and did you have a role in establishing that party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct -- after the HDZ was established in Croatia, a decision was adopted to go into the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and for this don Anto Bakovic and Perica Juric were put in charge of this job. I think that this job was done fairly quickly. The HDZ gained strength in Bosnia very quickly, precisely because a large number of Muslims also joined the HDZ there. The first President of the HDZ was Perinovic -- he is a physician. After that, there were certain personnel changes, but, also, the changes within the structure of the HDZ itself -- of the party -- so that people dropped out -- those people who were not part of the Croatian population dropped out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, was the HDZ political party in Croatia and the party in Bosnia related? Can you describe that relationship to the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the formal sense, I must say, for truth's sake, formally the HDZ in Croatia was separate from the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- that is formally, but, in reality, all decisions are made in Zagreb and I think that there is no doubt about it. I do not think that -- there is no question of the HDZ in Bosnia being an independent party in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- formally yes, but not in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you take the judges through the leadership of the HDZ political party in Bosnia, starting with Dr. Perinovic and identify who he was, what his ethnic background was, what his political philosophy was and take us through the succession of leaders in the HDZ political party in Bosnia, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before this first founding convention of the HDZ in Bosnia, it was not clear who was going to be its President. Don Anto Bakovic aspired to that position -- he is a Croat from Bosnia. However, the decision was made in Zagreb that Mr. Perinovic would be elected to that post. However, later, it was found out that he kept certain things from the public, that he had Serb background, that his ancestor was a priest of the Orthodox church, and it was not the fact that he was a Serb, but that he did not reveal this fact -- it was believed that he could then do that with things that were of interest for Croatia and so a new person was sought and Mr. Stjepan Kljujic was found, so he was elected President of the HDZ in Bosnia. I have to say that he was a tried and true advocate of Bosnia-Herzegovina as one State, and this put him on a collision course with those whose interests was not the same. I was given the role of replacing Mr. Kljujic at the meeting in Siroki Brijeg. I was present there and I told Mr. Kljujic that I was there, I was sent to relieve him of duty. However, in discussions with the executive board of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I realised that he had the full support of these people -- most of these people fully supported him, because the process of separation or division between the factions there had not yet taken place, that is, the faction that would advocate a separate Herceg-Bosna. I told him that, "When I go back to Zagreb, I will tell Mr. Franjo Tudjman that I could not relieve you of duty and that I had to leave the status quo there". However, Stjepan Kljujic said that, if Franjo Tudjman reached a decision to relieve him of duty, "He will do it one way or the other, so I am not going to resist this. I am going to resign and I am going to leave Siroki Brijeg and go to Sarajevo". I had no option but to seek a replacement for him. This was Miljenko Brkic, who was a university professor, a highly educated person who also was an advocate of a whole Herceg-Bosna. Today he is in Sarajevo and he stayed on this duty for several months and then a change took place, and he is replaced by Mate Boban. I had no part in that any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, let me ask you some questions about the parts of your testimony you have just concluded. You said that you were given the role to relieve Stjepan Kljujic as the head of the HDZ party in Bosnia; who gave you that role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same person who took the decision that Stjepan Kljujic should be elected President of the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that is the President of the HDZ for Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did he give you the role to relieve Stjepan Kljujic as the head of the HDZ party in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an objection from Bosnia-Herzegovina, conveyed to Zagreb, to the effect that Stjepan Kljujic did not sufficiently protect the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that he did not protect sufficiently the Croatian interests, that he did not advocate them sufficiently vehemently, and that he was a Croat actually under the control of Alija Izetbegovic, and for this reason a person should be sought who would be totally committed to the protection of Croatian interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mr. Mesic, Stjepan Kljujic was married to a Muslim woman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he still is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good. Now, eventually, you said that Mate Boban came to become the President of the HDZ political party in Bosnia. Can you tell the judges what his relationship was to Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before Boban, the acting President was Miljenko Brkic, after whom came Mate Boban. I must say that I was not too happy with this solution, though I knew Boban for many years, ever since the 60s -- 1967-68. He developed, or rather his political views developed from those of a man who was interested in democracy, to a man who started implementing policies which were imposed by Zagreb, or, rather, by Franjo Tudjman, and eventually he was totally committed to it and he implemented it. Whenever I spoke to him, he always said, and claimed, "I have no policies of my own. I am implementing what is expected of me from Zagreb -- what the President of the HDZ asks, is asking me to do". Unfortunately, that policy had its repercussions, but of a negative nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Mr. Boban tell you as well that he had to consult with Mr. Tudjman in respect of any important decision he took regarding Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said that, but even if he did not, the Croatian television broadcast daily images of people from the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina coming to Croatia. This could be seen daily on television, in the media, in the press. At first, these were visits by a delegation of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after which these visits became visits by delegations of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and now that is called a visit by a delegation of the Croatian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina calling on President Tudjman, but, in fact, they were always the same people coming to visit -- only the name has changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Mesic, could you please describe to the judges the political philosophy of the HDZ in Croatia at its inception, and how it evolved, and what it evolved to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the moment we accepted the new possibilities for the achievement of democracy in Croatia, until major divisions occurred, when we embarked upon the democratisation process, we said that affiliations with different Parties should not be considered, meaning that we were enemies amongst ourselves, simply because we belonged to different Parties, that we simply held different views about various problems and that is precisely why we belonged to different Parties, because we had different solutions to offer to those problems. And, when the HDZ was formed, this attitude was adopted. But, in time, as the movement did not -- was not transformed into a party, it was not structured as a party, there was a great deal of slowing down of democratisation which was eventually totally halted, and even the transformation of socially-owned property or social ownership was used to implement definite policies of the HDZ. Actually, for people who have not lived in our part of the world, it is difficult to understand what the term "social property" means and what its transformation implies. In fact, it was used for a robbery of the century such as probably not been seen anywhere else, namely, in the east and all the countries of transition, there was State property, only marginally private property and there was cooperative property. In the former Yugoslavia, we also had, in addition, "Social property", for which there is no affirmative definition. There is a negative definition only. "Social property" is described as not being cooperative or private or State property. The workers, through their workers' councils, managed a factory and an economic enterprise and the management board took care of the technology of the business side, headed by a manager, who was appointed by a certain mechanism, but the influence of the League of Communists was such that any enterprise of any significance -- the management of that enterprise was decided by the party committee. In principle, this social property made it possible for us to be closer to a market economy, closer to democratic societies, because, after all, these were economic entities that were relatively independent in decision-making, but the actual management of the enterprise was under the control of the party, or, rather, the League of Communists. In order to establish a society similar to that in the free world, we had to identify the owner. We had to establish who was in fact the owner, so that we could be compatible with western societies. This meant transforming this social property. In principle, we should have followed the trace to the source of the capital. In that case, the owners would be the former owners of the segment which would be worked out mathematically -- the owners whose property was nationalised under Communism; then the banks to whom loans were not returned, again, this could be calculated; and, finally, the workers who used to work in those enterprises would receive their shares through their pension funds, because they contributed to the capital of those enterprises, and then the present-day employees turn would come. That should have been the principle to be implemented. However, the HDZ leadership combined this transformation with privatisation, so that only fraudulent sales occurred, when individuals without a dollar in their pocket would purchase entire enterprises -- people who had no idea how to manage became managers, and what we had were people who destroyed the Croatian economy so that, among enterprises of significance, all that is left are warehouses with the workers being unemployed. The HDZ decided to grab capital while in power, and then, tomorrow, to continue to rule through ownership of capital. Of course, a key role was played in all this by the HDZ policy towards the media, which are absolutely, in the majority of cases, under the control of the HDZ, especially the electronic media and the TV. In that sense, the HDZ, as a movement, became an obstacle to the development of democracy, and, in that sense, it changed its appearance from the beginning, when it promised to struggle for democracy together with other courses, to become an element halting democratisation and imposing a new totalitarianism itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The HDZ political party in Bosnia, when it was founded, did it favour a sovereign Bosnian State and was it a party of inclusion; that is, it welcomed Serbs and Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is also evidence of this, because a large number of Muslims participated, and became members of the HDZ, so that, at the first elections, there was a concrete result -- if there were about 17 per cent Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and they won 24 per cent of the votes, this proves that a proportion of the Muslims, the Bosniaks had voted for the HDZ. At the time, when the HDZ for Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed, both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was a slogan to the effect that there can be no Bosnia-Herzegovina without Croatia and no Croatia without Bosnia-Herzegovina, but of course both were treated as Bosnian States.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The last question I have on this subject is, did the HDZ party in Bosnia change its philosophy and become a party which had aspirations that favoured integration into Croatia, and excluded Muslims and Serbs from participating in the party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say, due to the considerable pressure from the Milosevic regime, brought to bear on the Serbs in Croatia and the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were few Serbs in the HDZ. There were some -- formally they could become members, but neither did the Croats accept them as members, nor did they themselves want to join the HDZ, because they would have been accused by the Serbs of being traitors, whereas cooperation with the Bosniaks, the Muslims at first was excellent. We even organised the training of policemen from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a large number of those policemen were actually Muslims. However, as power in the HDZ was taken over by those who were not genuinely interested in the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who kept speaking about Croatian areas and never about Bosnia-Herzegovina, and who finally imposed a policy -- not a policy of co-existence but a policy of separate existence by Serbs, Croats and Muslims, namely, a thesis came to the fore that Serbs, Croats and Muslims in Bosnia could not live together and that a separation had to occur. There were many things that contributed to this, one of them being that, within the circles who were against the survival of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was being said that Bosnia-Herzegovina was, how should I put it, an entity which is unfeasible in the same way that the former Yugoslavia was unfeasible and that is why it collapsed, and so that Bosnia-Herzegovina was also unfeasible, it was not a logical community, and, for that reason, the parts had to separate. However, this thesis is subject to serious criticism, and one of those criticisms is that Bosnia did not come into being when Yugoslavia came into being; it was formed a long time ago by populations, who had lived in a multi-cultural, multi-ethnic multi-religious environment, and the hatred did not occur because they suddenly decided to separate and to go their separate ways and form their own States. The hatred was only the product of the war. It needs to be overcome. It does indeed exist but it was encouraged from the outside in the first place, by Milosevic's policy of breaking up Bosnia-Herzegovina, because, I must say, I do not know whether you are familiar with this, but, according to the 1974 constitution, which was passed by Tito, after suppressing the Croatian Spring, but having endorsed the thesis from the Croatian Spring that Yugoslavia could survive after Tito but only as a confederal model and, according to that constitution, the Republics were the sovereign entities and they were entitled to become independent if the federation could not survive. Therefore, the Yugoslavia federation was called a federation, but by the constitution of 1974 it had evolved into a confederation and Milosevic was actually doing tricks. He was tricking all the peoples of the former Yugoslavia and then also the international community and the European and international organisations by claiming that it was the right of the nations to independence, which would mean that the parts of Croatia inhabited by Serbs could be annexed to greater Serbia and especially so parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- all these could, in the future, form this future greater Serbia. Clearly, this was in contradiction with the constitution and it was not feasible, because the right to independence, according to the constitution, was enjoyed by the Republics and this was something that was eventually confirmed by the Badinter Commission and it is on those grounds we have independent States, Croatia within its borders, Macedonia within its borders and Slovenia within its borders and a wounded Bosnia within its borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have concluded my examination. If we are to conclude at 6, this would be an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will suspend the hearing now, and start again tomorrow at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: at 2.30pm)
